diagnosis: New-Onset Atrial Fibrillation with Rapid Ventricular Response

patient.key: 65F, chest pain + palpitations + dizziness. History of anxiety disorder (taking alprazolam PRN) and HTN. Recent stressors. EKG: AF with RVR. TSH and T3/T4 all normal. Echo: mild LA enlargement, EF 65%, no thrombus. HR rapid on presentation, symptomatically improved after IV metoprolol. Spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm. CHA2DS2-VASc = 3 (female +1, age >=65 +1, HTN +1) → anticoagulation indicated.

ekg: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response
echo: Mild left atrial enlargement, no LAA thrombus, EF 65%, normal valves and wall motion

cha2ds2vasc.recommendation: Score >=2 in women → oral anticoagulation strongly recommended (DOAC preferred)

appropriateOrders.note: Ordered 'Ablation, tumor' — considered invasive for this case. Ablation is for recurrent symptomatic AF, not new-onset in ED.

correctlyOrdered: Physical Exam: General, Chest/Lungs, Heart, HEENT/Neck (thyroid exam), Neuro/Psych
Echocardiography (optional but good practice — LAE, no thrombus, EF 65%)

missedOrders.order: Anticoagulation (warfarin / DOAC: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran)
missedOrders.why: CHA2DS2-VASc = 3 → yearly stroke risk ~3-5%. Guidelines strongly recommend OAC. DOACs are first-line over warfarin. Aspirin alone reduces stroke risk by only 20-25% vs ~60-70% with OAC. Aspirin + clopidogrel (ACTIVE-A) still far short of OAC. The entire point of the AF diagnosis is stroke prevention.

Need baseline coagulation status before starting anticoagulation. No prior thromboembolism, so heparin bridge is NOT needed — but baseline PT/PTT is standard of care before initiating any anticoagulant.
Screening tool. Also: anemia affects DOAC dosing and bleeding risk stratification.
Renal function is critical — creatinine clearance determines which DOACs are appropriate and at what dose. Electrolytes may reveal hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia contributing to AF.
AF patient needs continuous rhythm monitoring. Can detect conversion to sinus vs deterioration to unstable rhythm.
Oxygenation check in a distressed patient.
Abdominal pathology can contribute to dizziness/chest discomfort.
Check for edema — sign of heart failure that would change management.
Substance use (cocaine, amphetamines) can cause palpitations and AF. Patient already on alprazolam (potential for misuse).

missedPrevention: Tdap vaccine (every 10 years, no history given)

wrongDecisions.why: Cost 0% on Appropriate Orders. Ablation is an elective rhythm-control strategy for RECURRENT symptomatic AF refractory to medication — not for new-onset AF in the ED. The patient spontaneously converted to sinus rhythm after rate control. Ablation is a cardiology subspecialty decision made weeks to months later, not an ED order.

pathophysiology.afRvr: Atrial fibrillation: chaotic, rapid atrial electrical activity (400-600 bpm) with irregular conduction through the AV node → irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm. Rapid ventricular response = ventricular rate >100 bpm. Symptoms: palpitations, chest pain (from demand ischemia), dizziness (from reduced cardiac output — loss of atrial kick).
pathophysiology.rateVsRhythm: Acute management in a STABLE patient = rate control (beta-blocker or CCB). Rhythm control (cardioversion) is for UNSTABLE patients (hypotension, shock, acute heart failure) or elective management. This patient was stable — BP normal, no heart failure — so rate control was correct.
pathophysiology.anticoagulation: AF causes blood stasis in the left atrium (especially the LAA) → thrombus formation → cardioembolic stroke. CHA2DS2-VASc quantifies stroke risk. Score >=2 = OAC recommended. The paradox of AF: the arrhythmia is annoying but rarely fatal; the stroke is devastating and entirely preventable.
pathophysiology.doacVsWarfarin: DOACs (apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran): direct factor Xa or thrombin inhibitors, fixed dosing, no INR monitoring, fewer drug interactions, faster onset, at least as effective as warfarin with less intracranial hemorrhage. Warfarin: vitamin K antagonist, requires INR monitoring, many drug/food interactions, but well-established and reversible. Heparin bridge is NOT needed for new-onset AF without prior thromboembolism — start OAC directly.
pathophysiology.laEnlargement: Mild LAE is a structural consequence of AF (or a predisposing factor). It reflects the atrial remodeling that makes AF more likely to sustain itself ('AF begets AF'). LAE also increases stroke risk independently.
pathophysiology.spontaneousConversion: Up to 70% of new-onset AF converts spontaneously to sinus rhythm within 24-48 hours, especially after rate control reduces atrial stretch and sympathetic tone. This patient did convert — metoprolol worked.

teachingPoints: The most dangerous thing about AF is not the arrhythmia — it's the stroke. Rate control manages symptoms. Anticoagulation prevents death and disability.
CHA2DS2-VASc drives the decision. Score 3 → OAC. DOAC first-line. Not aspirin. Not DAPT. Oral anticoagulation.
PT/PTT before starting AC — baseline coagulation status. Not for heparin bridging (that's for high-risk patients transitioning to warfarin). Just for baseline.
Renal function (BMP) determines DOAC choice and dose. CKD → dose adjustment or warfarin.
Ablation is not an ED order. It's a subspecialty decision for recurrent symptomatic AF after medication failure. Ordering it in the ED = invasive penalty.
Thyroid labs make sense but were normal in this case. Always check TSH in new AF — hyperthyroidism is a reversible cause.
The anxiety history is a trap. Yes, she has anxiety. No, that doesn't mean her palpitations are a panic attack. AF and anxiety can coexist. Rule out the arrhythmia first.
